name: How the canon was formed
source: Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible: Its Formation, History, and Fluctuations (3rd revised ed., New York: Peter Eckler, 1877; Project Gutenberg eBook 30132)
licence: Public domain; passages quoted with their printed page numbers; scripture quoted from the ESV
note: Commentary written for this site; the source is named on the Sources page.

entries.title: The Law, the Prophets and the Psalms: Luke 24:44
entries.content:
Luke has the risen Jesus name three parts of scripture. The Law of Moses and the Prophets are the first two. The third is called the Psalms, which is the largest book of the writings and the one that gave the whole division its name.

Then he said to them, “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.”

Luke 24:44

A fixed list, or a loose one?

Davidson, writing in 1877, finds the same pattern. He writes that the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms were “universally recognized as authoritative; but the extent of the third division was indefinite.”

It is true that the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms were universally recognized as authoritative; but the extent of the third division was indefinite

Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (1877), p. 52

That fits the lists that survive. Josephus, near the end of the first century, counts twenty-two books, a number Davidson says was “the usual number among Christian writers in the second, third, and fourth centuries.” The Tanakh counts twenty-four for the same writings. The count changes and the books do not.

Read this way, Luke 24:44 names the shape of the scriptures Jesus knew. It does not give a list of titles, and it leaves open which books sat in the third part.

Source: Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (1877), pp. 28, 48, 52. See Sources.

entries.title: Jude quotes Enoch: Jude 1:14-15
entries.content:
Jude names a prophecy of Enoch and quotes it. The words are found in the Book of Enoch, an older Jewish writing that is not in the Hebrew Bible, and that Davidson says is not in the Alexandrian canon, the Greek list of the Jews of Alexandria.

It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, “Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.”

Jude 1:14-15

What Davidson makes of it

Davidson draws a narrow conclusion. He says Jude “quotes Enoch, an apocryphal work not in the Alexandrian canon; so that he at least had no rigid notions about the difference of canonical and uncanonical writings.”

Jude quotes Enoch, an apocryphal work not in the Alexandrian canon; so that he at least had no rigid notions about the difference of canonical and uncanonical writings.

Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (1877), p. 52

Where Enoch stayed

Enoch turns up again in the lists of the Eastern churches. In his survey of the Syrian, Ethiopic and Armenian canons Davidson says later catalogues “vary much, and are often enlarged with the book of Enoch, 4 Esdras, the Apocalypse of Isaiah”, and adds: “The canon of the Ethiopic church was fluctuating.” One verse in a short letter was enough to put the question of the edges of scripture on the table.

Source: Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (1877), pp. 52, 105. See Sources.

entries.title: An echo of Wisdom: Hebrews 1:3
entries.content:
The opening of Hebrews describes the Son in words that some readers hear as an echo of the Book of Wisdom, which speaks of wisdom as a reflection of God at work. The ESV text has no Wisdom of Solomon, so the parallel is set out here in words, and Wisdom 7:26 can be read in any Bible that carries it.

He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,

Hebrews 1:3

An echo is a weaker thing than a citation

Davidson lists this verse among the supposed allusions to the apocrypha that the scholar Bleek kept after cutting a much longer list: “Hebrews i. 3, from Wisdom vii. 26.” He adds that the others are “less probable.”

Hebrews i. 3, from Wisdom vii. 26, &c.

Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (1877), p. 51

He also reports the argument of Bishop Cosin that no passage of the apocryphal books is “alleged either by Christ or His apostles for the confirmation of their doctrine.” Davidson calls the argument “based on fact” and “scarcely conclusive”, since the same test would discredit Esther and the Song of Songs.

The sound reading is that Hebrews shares a vocabulary with a book the church later put in a different place. It does not quote it by name, and the verse proves a shared vocabulary only.

Source: Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (1877), p. 51. See Sources.

entries.title: Does Revelation close the Bible? Revelation 22:18-19
entries.content:
The book ends with a warning against adding to its words or taking from them. Readers often take it as a seal on the whole Bible. The warning speaks of “the words of the prophecy of this book”, which is the book of Revelation.

I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book, and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.

Revelation 22:18-19

A seal on the Bible that some churches had not yet accepted

The churches did not agree for centuries that Revelation belonged in the list at all. Davidson reports a list of New Testament books attached to the 60th canon of the Council of Laodicea that is complete except for it: “The Apocalypse alone is wanting.” He adds that Credner “has proved that this 60th canon is not original, and of much later date”, so the list shows a later Greek habit more than a decision of that council.

The Apocalypse alone is wanting.

Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (1877), p. 88

Of Amphilochius of Iconium he says the New Testament list “agrees with the present, only he excludes the Apocalypse as spurious; which is given as the judgment of the majority.”

His New Testament canon agrees with the present, only he excludes the Apocalypse as spurious; which is given as the judgment of the majority.

Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (1877), p. 91

A verse that ends one book cannot also close a collection that had not been gathered when it was written, and that some of the churches reading it still left incomplete.

Source: Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (1877), pp. 88, 91. See Sources.
